extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in geometric topology and the Poincaré conjecture
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarizing the Poincaré conjecture: its precise statement for 3-manifolds, historical attempts, key intermediate criteria (Ricci flow, singularity types, finite extinction), and results (Perelman's proof and higher-dimensional analogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré conjecture (statement for 3-manifolds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every three-dimensional topological manifold which is closed, connected, and has trivial fundamental group is homeomorphic to the three-dimensional sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and implications appear in the article: 'closed' means no boundary and finite extent, 'connected' means a single piece, and 'trivial fundamental group' means every loop can be continuously tightened to a point. The two-dimensional analogue is true and illustrated by the sphere vs. torus example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-dimensional analogue / classification of closed surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: In two dimensions, the classification of closed and connected surfaces implies that any closed connected 2-manifold not homeomorphic to the 2-sphere must possess a loop which cannot be continuously contracted to a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as motivation and contrast: the torus has nontrivial fundamental group while the sphere does not; the 2D case has been understood since the 19th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized Poincaré conjecture (higher dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n ≥ 3 one can ask: is a homotopy n-sphere homeomorphic to the n-sphere? In dimensions >4 Smale proved the generalized conjecture; Freedman proved the 4-dimensional topological version; the smooth 4D case remains open and exotic spheres show the smooth Poincaré conjecture is false in some dimensions (e.g., dimension 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that simply-connectedness is not a strong enough hypothesis in higher dimensions and that different categories (topological, PL, smooth) have different status/results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton's positive Ricci curvature criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a compact simply-connected 3-manifold supports a Riemannian metric of positive Ricci curvature, then it must be diffeomorphic to the 3-sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton showed that under Ricci flow (with appropriate scaling ct g(t)) such metrics converge smoothly to one of constant positive curvature as t approaches a finite time T, and classical Riemannian geometry then implies the manifold is the sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricci flow with surgery — singularity classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularities that appear in Ricci flow (on 3-manifolds) can only look like shrinking spheres or cylinders, allowing the manifold to be cut along those singularities and capped; Perelman proved the singularities are sufficiently simple to permit surgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perelman's analysis (using the Reduced Volume and other tools) shows that troublesome singularities (e.g., the cigar soliton) do not occur in the obstructive form, so one can split the manifold into pieces and continue Ricci flow on each piece (the 'Ricci flow with surgery' procedure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite extinction criterion for Ricci flow with surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: On a simply-connected compact 3-manifold any solution of the Ricci flow with surgery becomes extinct in finite time. More generally, finite-time extinction occurs exactly when the fundamental group is a free product of finite groups and cyclic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic condition on the fundamental group is equivalent to the prime decomposition having no acyclic components and to all geometric pieces having geometries based on S^2×R and S^3; finite-time extinction is the key property used to deduce the Poincaré conclusion in the simply-connected case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's Reduced Volume / entropy monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Perelman introduced the 'Reduced Volume' (entropy formula) and proved monotonicity properties (an eigenvalue-like quantity goes up) as the manifold is deformed by Ricci flow, which was used to rule out certain problematic singularity models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This monotonicity helped eliminate the cigar soliton-type singularity and showed that 'strands' that form can be cut and capped without leaving one-sided protrusions, a crucial technical input to the surgery program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal surfaces area argument to prevent infinite surgeries
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a minimal surface decreases under Ricci flow (a result of Hamilton); Perelman analyzed what happens to minimal surfaces when the manifold is sliced and used this to show that one cannot require infinitely many surgeries — eventually further cuts only remove round 3-spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perelman's third paper contains the argument that bounds the number of necessary surgeries by showing the area becomes so small that only spherical pieces can be removed thereafter (often described metaphorically as a battle with a Hydra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricci flow program strategy (Hamilton → Perelman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program: equip the 3-manifold with a Riemannian metric, evolve it by Ricci flow to 'improve' the metric; understand and control singularities (via classification and surgery); show the process terminates in round pieces so the manifold can be reconstructed as the 3-sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces Hamilton's original program and Perelman's completion: Perelman modified Hamilton's approach, provided new techniques and results (reduced volume, singularity analysis, finite extinction), and showed how to carry out surgery to obtain the Poincaré and geometrization conclusions.
